title: Cache fidelity calibration harness and regression notes
summary: Design notes and experimental log for a lightweight harness that calibrates how closely the microbench and synthetic traces match production KV cache behavior. Captures guidance for scheduling policies and regression detection thresholds when KV hit-rate varies.
body:
Purpose:

This doc captures the design and running notes for a calibration harness intended to: 1) measure how microbench results change as we vary KV cache fidelity (hit-rate distributions, TTL churn, prefix overlap); 2) produce a compact regression signal that ties kernel selection and scheduling policy changes back to observable latency/p99 regressions; and 3) provide reproducible recipes to generate augmented traces that mimic target workloads for nightly CI and dev experimentation.

Background / motivation:

We have a gap between microbench numbers (synthetic workloads hitting a small KV working set) and production traces where KV hit patterns are bursty and correlated with particular routes. When we tune (a) kernel selection heuristics, (b) scheduler batching windows, or (c) prefix caching heuristics, small changes that look benign on microbench can cause 10–30% tail regressions on real traces. The harness below tries to bridge that gap by parameterizing cache fidelity and explicitly exercising scheduler degeneracies.

Core ideas and components:

- KV fidelity model: programmatic generator that can replay or synthesize hit/miss sequences. Parameters: mean hit-rate, burstiness (burst length), working set size, TTL churn rate, and prefix overlap factor.
- Trace augmentation: take a real production trace (sampled mini-trace ~2000 requests) and inject synthetic KV noise: we overlay additional misses/hits at controlled rates, splice in longer sequences to emulate long-context re-requests, and randomly shift request timings to simulate coalescing-induced batching.
- Microbench variants: small focused benches for (1) pure-kernel latency (single-infer no kv), (2) kv-hot path (high hit-rate), (3) kv-cold path (high miss-rate + kv population churn), (4) mixed schedule stress (many small requests arriving close together).
- Scheduler stress harness: runs multiple traffic classes simultaneously (e.g., foreground low-latency vs background throughput) to surface preemption and priority inversion problems under different KV fidelity settings.
- Signal extraction: compute p50/p95/p99 latency, cold-start tail, token/s, GPU kernel launch counts, average kernel runtime, and kv-lookup CPU latency. Also capture distribution of batch sizes seen by runtime and number of KV lookups per request.

Instrumentation checklist (what to capture from the runtime):

- request_id, route, model_version, trace_id
- kv_lookup_count, kv_lookup_latency_ms (per-request histogram)
- pre-batch queue depth, batch_formation_time_ms
- kernel_launch_count, kernel_time_ms (per kernel type)
- GPU occupancy / SM utilization (from nsys or nvprof samples tied to request window)
- host CPU stolen time, syscalls per request (to catch lock contention)

Experiment matrix (first pass):

Each run: a baseline microbench run (no KV churn), augmented trace run (moderate churn), and worst-case run (high churn + high burstiness). Repeat for scheduler policy permutations.

Parameters to sweep:

- mean_hit_rate: [0.95, 0.8, 0.6, 0.3]
- burstiness(B): [1 (Poisson-like), 4, 16] where B is expected consecutive hits/misses
- ttl_churn: [stable, 1%/min, 5%/min]
- working_set_size: [small (10k entries), medium (100k), large (1M)]
- scheduler_policy: [fifo, adaptive-window-16, adaptive-window-64, priority-preempt]
- batch_window_ms: [2, 6, 12]
- kernel_backoff: [enabled, disabled] (this toggles the runtime's heuristic to force smaller kernels when occupancy low)

Primary hypotheses to validate:

1) Lower hit-rate increases average request KV latency but disproportionately increases p99 when burstiness is high (due to batching delays and KV miss fanout).
2) Adaptive-window scheduler tuned for low batches (window=6ms) shows best p50 under high hit-rate, but p99 regresses when hit-rate drops because the runtime forms unexpectedly large batches that incur heavier kernel runtimes.
3) Kernel backoff mitigates some p99 regressions at the expense of throughput; we can quantify break-even points (hit_rate threshold where backoff becomes net-positive).

Representative run log (selected runs):

RUN A (baseline)
- params: mean_hit_rate=0.95, B=1, working_set=10k, scheduler=adaptive-window-16, window=6ms
- metrics: p50=18ms, p95=34ms, p99=78ms, tokens/s=1200, avg_batch=3.2
- note: lightweight, matches microbench expectations

RUN B (augmented trace)
- params: mean_hit_rate=0.6, B=4, working_set=100k, scheduler=adaptive-window-16, window=6ms
- metrics: p50=22ms, p95=58ms, p99=210ms, tokens/s=820, avg_batch=7.8
- observation: p99 ballooned. Kernel launch counts spiked (20% more launches of the large attention kernel), GPU occupancy trend shows extended kernel durations consistent with larger batches.

RUN C (high burst, different scheduler)
- params: mean_hit_rate=0.6, B=16, working_set=100k, scheduler=priority-preempt, window=12ms
- metrics: p50=26ms, p95=120ms, p99=410ms, tokens/s=600, avg_batch=12.4
- observation: priority-preempt reduced average p50 for high-priority routes but had starvation effects on lower-priority work. We observed a lock in the KV client causing 1.2% of requests to timeout after 3s in this configuration (investigate KV client locking).

Regression detection rules proposed for CI:

- For any PR touching scheduler/kernel heuristics run the 3-case matrix (baseline, augmented, worst-case). Fail if:
  - p99 increases by >20% in augmented or worst-case vs baseline run (after accounting for noise with 5 repeats), OR
  - tokens/s decreases by >15% in augmented run, OR
  - avg_batch grows by >2x with correlated p95/p99 increases

Repro steps (quick):

1) checkout runtimes repo + harness branch: git checkout pr/harness-cache-fidelity
2) Setup local kv-sim: python tools/kv_sim/server.py --entries=100000 --latency-ms=0.8
3) Run calibration script: python tools/harness/run_calibration.py --trace samples/mini_prod_trace.json --mean_hit_rate 0.6 --burstiness 4 --out runs/run_b.json
4) Collect metrics: ./tools/harness/collect_metrics.sh runs/run_b.json --dest ./artifacts/run_b/
5) Visualize: python tools/harness/plot_run.py ./artifacts/run_b/metrics.json

Quick commands (dev-friendly):

- Start local KV sim (simple, no auth): python -m tools.kv_sim --entries 100000 --p99 2.5
- Run single microbench case: ./bazel-bin/tools/bench/microbench --case=kv-hot --n=2000 --out=out.json
- Fire an augmented trace: python tools/harness/replay_trace.py --trace samples/mini_prod_trace.json --aug-rate 0.4 --burst 8

Known issues and caveats:

- Current kv_sim is single-threaded; it underestimates contention compared to prod (we see less syscall overhead). We should add a threaded mode to simulate concurrent client threads.
- GPU occupancy numbers currently captured by periodic nsys snapshots; this loses per-request correlation when batch spans snapshot boundaries. We need event tracing at the request-to-kernel level.
- Bias introduced by short mini-trace lengths: a 2000-request sample misses diurnal effects. For nightly CI we should include at least one 20k-request sample (costs ~6h to run in CI unless we parallelize).
- The harness currently ignores function/tool-call latencies; in prod, tool calls often cause KV miss cascades. We should model that in a follow-up.

Action items (owners and next steps):

- Add threaded kv_sim option to emulate client-side concurrency and connection pooling (owner: Jared Kim, ETA: 2024-10-18).
- Implement per-request GPU event tagging in runtime and wire it to harness (owner: Mikhail Orlov, ETA: 2024-10-25).
- Add nightly CI job that runs the 3-case matrix on a small dedicated GPU node and stores artifacts for 14 days (owner: Priya Nair, ETA: 2024-11-05).
- Investigate KV client locking observed in RUN C (owner: Elena Park, immediate).

Appendix: sample small metrics dump (abridged)

- summary: {
  "run_id": "run_b", "mean_hit_rate": "0.6", "burstiness": "4"
}
- p50_ms: 22
- p95_ms: 58
- p99_ms: 210
- avg_batch: 7.8
- tokens_s: 820
- kernel_launches: attention_large=21432, attention_small=12190

Notes to self:

- Keep cross-referencing this harness output with real postmortems where kv-miss-induced tails were a factor. I want to build a tiny dashboard that surfaces runs whose p99 shows modal shifts rather than monotonic drift (i.e., heavy tail vs small constant offset).
- Consider adding a synthetic "prefix re-use" model that simulates multi-turn sessions with increasing prefix overlap — this is likely important for chat-like workloads.

If you run this locally and see unexpected p99 spikes, paste the artifacts dir into #eng-runtime and tag me.
notes: Draft meant to be actionable; contains runnable commands and clear owners. Avoid using for public distribution until harness stabilizes.
